source_text: Acta quidem res est; sed tamen, ut ad id quod affero sit intentus lector, admoneo. Si quispiam exsisteret, qui hoc profiteretur libertate verborum, quod argumentando Traducianus conficere conatur, id est ut pugnam indiceret legi Dei et sententiam, quam protulimus, sine aliquo timore despiceret assereretque, quibus posset modis, falsum hoc utrumque esse, quod Deus servari voluit, et sententiam, de qua loquimur, ex utraque, quantum in se erat, parte subrueret, prorsus putasset parentes propter filiorum et filios propter parentum peccata tam solere quam debere damnari, nec hic tamen talis peccati traducem, vel secundum opiniones suas quiret asserere. Cur? Videlicet quia, etsi constaret falsam legis esse sententiam, quae testificaretur eiusmodi necessitudines respergi mutuis non posse criminibus, tamen inconcussum manebat traducem non esse peccati. Hoc enim ipso, quo et parentum reatus ad filios et filiorum ad parentes redibat, constabat non fuisse generationis, quod ad filios gignentium peccata pervenerant, quoniam et a filiis ad parentes, ubi generatio non poterat causa esse, remeaverant. Quid igitur hic confecerim appareat, inviolabilem quidem esse auctoritatem legis divinae et quam nulla queant impietatum argumenta proruere, eius autem sanctione signantissime atque absolutissime fuisse praescriptum foedam esse opinionem perversitatemque iudicii, quam mandaverat vehementer cavendam, si rei filii pro peccato pronuntiarentur parentum, quo fulmine traducis structura dissiluit, verumtamen tantis esse veritatis praesidiis munitam quam tuemur fidem, ut nec ab ea profanitate, quae potest Dei legem negare, quatiatur.
pass_a_gloss: The matter has indeed been transacted; but nevertheless, that the reader may be intent on what I bring, I warn. If anyone existed who would profess with freedom of words what the advocate of inherited sin tries to accomplish by arguing, that is that he would declare war on the law of God and without any fear despise the sentence we have brought forth and would assert by whatever modes he could that both things God wanted to be kept are false, and would, as far as was in him, undermine from both sides the sentence of which we speak, and would have thought parents on account of sons' sins and sons on account of parents' sins both are accustomed and ought to be condemned, not even here could such a one assert a vine-layer of sin, even according to his own opinions. Why? Namely because, even if it stood that the law's sentence was false which testified that kinships of this kind cannot be sprinkled with mutual crimes, nevertheless it remained unshaken that there is not a vine-layer of sin. For by this very thing, that both parents' guilt returned to sons and sons' to parents, it stood that it was not of generation that generating persons' sins had reached sons, since they had also gone back from sons to parents, where generation could not be the cause. What therefore I have accomplished here let it appear: that the authority of the divine law is inviolable and such as no arguments of impieties can overthrow, but that by its sanction it was most signally and most absolutely prescribed that the foul opinion and perversity of judgment is what it had commanded to be vehemently avoided, if sons were pronounced defendants for the sin of parents, by which thunderbolt the structure of the vine-layer burst apart; yet that the faith we guard is fortified by such defenses of truth that it is not shaken even by that profanity which can deny God's law.

lemmas.lexica: Blaise Traduciani=those who teach tradux peccati; not merely traducianism of the soul
LS tradux=vine-shoot/layer; Blaise tradux peccati=transmission of sin by descent
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin

pass_b_english: The case is settled. Still, I urge the reader to attend to what I now bring forward. Suppose someone openly professed what the advocate of inherited sin tries to establish by argument: suppose he declared war on God’s law, fearlessly despised the pronouncement we quoted, and asserted, by whatever means he could, that both requirements God wished observed were false. Suppose he did all he could to overthrow both sides of the pronouncement under discussion and fully believed that parents are and ought to be condemned for their children’s sins, and children for their parents’. Even a person like that could not establish the transmission of sin, even on his own assumptions. Why? Because even if the law’s pronouncement were proved false—the pronouncement testifying that relatives of this kind cannot be stained by each other’s crimes—it would remain unshaken that sin is not transmitted. The very fact that parental guilt passed to children and children’s guilt returned to parents would establish that birth was not what brought parents’ sins to children, since they also returned from children to parents, where birth could not be the cause.

Let the result of my argument be clear. Divine law has an inviolable authority, which no arguments of impiety can overthrow. Its decree prescribed with the greatest precision and completeness that declaring children guilty for their parents’ sin is a disgraceful opinion and a distortion of judgment, which it commanded us earnestly to avoid. This thunderbolt shattered the structure of inherited sin. Yet the faith we defend is protected by such strong defenses of truth that even the irreverence capable of denying God’s law cannot shake it.

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Julian's label for teachers of tradux peccati. Keep the polemic name as a description of transmitted sin, not as a theory of the soul's origin.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: Continues the explicit argument from the law forbidding punishment of parents and children for one another’s sins.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
